            Daniel Oropeza
                
                                            Shopping Editor

    Table of Contents
    
        
        Pet hair tends to gather in inconvenient and less conspicuous places—along baseboards, under furniture, and on upholstery—which can make dragging out a full-size upright vacuum feel like more trouble than the mess warrants. The cordless Bissell PowerClean DualBrush is designed for these routine cleanups, and it is currently on sale for $199.99 (originally $359.99). That is a $160 savings.Beyond pet-related messes, the PowerClean can also pick up crumbs, dust, tracked-in dirt, and other debris that accumulates between more thorough cleaning sessions. Because it converts from a standard stick vacuum into a handheld model and works with several attachments, you can move from cleaning floors to tackling furniture, stairs, and narrow spaces without reaching for a different machine. That versatility carries over to the way it cleans: Two self-cleaning brush rolls handle everything from scattered pet food to finer particles like fur and dust, while Bissell’s AutoAdapt system increases the suction when it detects a dirtier spot, allowing you to continue across the room without repeatedly stopping to manually change modes.The headlights on the floorhead add another practical touch, helping expose pale fur on rugs and fine dust on hard floors as you move around the room. That said, while Bissell says the battery can last up to 50 minutes, that estimate applies only when the detachable handheld vacuum is running in its lowest-power mode—and using stronger suction or the motorized floorhead will reduce that runtime. The 0.4-liter dust cup is another limitation, particularly in homes with several shedding pets, where it may need to be emptied during a longer cleaning session. These small compromises aside, the PowerClean will suit anyone who needs a cordless vacuum that can cover floors, stairs, furniture, and pet beds without requiring much setup or a full-size machine, especially at its current $160 discount.
            
                What do you think so far?

title: Amazon's New 'About You' Page Lists Everything It Knows About You

body:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
        
        It shouldn't come as a surprise that Amazon collects data about you based on what you buy. And now, you can get a direct look at what the company has concluded from all that activity.Amazon's "About You" page, currently in beta after launching this May, uses data from customers' activity to generate details about them in categories like Product Preferences, Interests & Hobbies, and Home & Family. Amazon uses those details to personalize the shopping experience. Here's how to navigate and personalize your "About You" page in your Amazon account.What Amazon thinks it knows about youThe results can be oddly specific. My editor-in-chief, Jordan Calhoun, shared his page, which includes these entries:
"Likely has 2 adults""Owns a PlayStation 5 console""Prioritizes plant-based meat alternatives over traditional options""Subscribes to multiple streaming services continually""Owns a large dog""Likely has a cat"Full disclosure: I try to never use Amazon personally. I pretty much exclusively use it to round up deals for you, my dear reader. That being said, here's what Amazon thinks it knows about me: "Values durable travel gear," "prefers athletic and casual clothing styles," "practices yoga regularly," and "listens to music frequently."What counts as dataIn its Privacy Notice, Amazon lists every activity that provides user data to the company. That includes the obvious, like searching for items and placing orders. It also includes actions you may not realize are being tracked, like interacting with Alexa Voice Service, participating in discussion boards, or linking an Amazon account to a third-party business.How to view your own "About you" pageOn desktop:Hover over where Amazon says "Hello, [your name]" in the upper right corner.Under the "Your Account" section, click "Account."Under the "Ordering and shopping preferences" section, click "Your Shopping preferences."From here, you can add information of your own, like your shoe size, interests, and dietary preferences. Scroll to the bottom of the page, and you'll see a blue hyperlinked option that says, "Manage your information." Click it, and you'll see what dirt Amazon has on you.On the mobile app:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Tap the hamburger icon in the bottom menu bar, then go to Account > Shopping preferences > About you.You can edit it, but not opt outShoppers can't directly opt out of the "About you" feature. They can, however, customize the data by adding details they want Amazon to know and deleting assumptions they consider inaccurate or too personal.Importing data from other AI chatbotsOn the "About you" page, customers also have the option to "make Amazon even more personal to you" by importing personal data they've shared with other AI agents. Amazon provides a prompt for you to feed to your chatbot to generate a shopping profile, then asks you to copy the bot's response and paste it back into Amazon.Whether that's worth doing is up to you. Given how much Amazon already infers from your browsing and buying, handing over a profile from another AI service is a choice worth thinking through. Either way, taking a few minutes to review your page and delete anything inaccurate or too personal is a simple way to see and shape what Amazon knows about you.

title: Ring Designed a Keyless Smart Lock That Can Still Open When the Battery Dies
body:
Joel Cunningham
                            
        
            Joel Cunningham
                
                                            Deputy Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJoel Cunningham is Lifehacker’s Deputy Editor. He has 15 years of experience as a writer and editor. Previously, he was managing editor of content marketing for Barnes & Noble, where he founded the Barnes & Noble Sci-Fi & Fantasy Blog.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        October 7, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Joel Cunningham
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        This past summer, I replaced the deadbolt on my front door with a smart lock, and it's possibly the best house upgrade I've ever made. I'm still not over the convenience of being able to leave the house without worrying about where my keys are, or if my absent kids have their keys. The only thing I need to worry about is the battery going dead, as that means the, uh, deadbolt will, too; thus, I still need to make copies of the manual key and figure out where to hide it in case of a lockout. But what if there was a smart lock that you could open without a key, even if the batteries were totally drained?Turns out that Ring built one, and the concept behind it is as simple as it is ingenious. In the first quarter of 2027, the Amazon-owned company, whose name is synonymous with video doorbells, will release its first-ever smart lock, and it will include a truly innovative feature: a built-in "Power Dial" that will allow you to manually generate enough energy to quickly unlock your door, even if the battery is totally dead—no manual key required. I got a chance to preview the mechanism at a meeting with Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, and I walked away kicking myself that I didn't wait to get one.Why Ring's "Power Dial" will stand out among smart locks
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Ring / Amazon
                    
    
According to Siminoff, Ring had long resisted stepping into the smart lock market, as he saw no real upside in dropping another virtually identical product into an overcrowded market. But then, when trying to choose a smart lock for his own guest home, located in a remote area, he couldn't find a device he wanted: one that would work reliably every time, even if no one had been at the house to change the batteries, and that didn't require worrying about hiding a backup key in a fake rock somewhere. So he designed one.Inspired by those battery-free flashlights that charge via friction when you turn a crank, Siminoff sketched out plans for a rotating dial built directly into the lock's keypad that could generate enough energy to open it after just a few seconds spent turning it back and forth. Once recharged, the lock will open in all the usual smart lock ways: with a numerical code, or a fingerprint, or the Ring app, or an Alexa request.
The Power Dial is a way to "get rid of [the need for a] backup key without the anxiety," said Siminoff, who noted that, considering the pace of technological development (he's able to turn on his Tesla using his phone), "it's insane that we still use keys [to enter our homes]"—pin tumbler locks being essentially unchanged from technology invented nearly 200 years ago. With no keyhole that can be picked, a smart lock can also be that much more secure.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Despite this innovation, when it comes to market early next year (after receiving FCC approval), Ring's smart lock will cost about the same as its competitors, around $250 in one of three finishes (brass, stainless steel, or black). There's no exact release date yet.Ring is also releasing a new line of security cameras
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Image courtesy of Ring / Amazon
                    
    
In addition to the new lock, Ring has also announced an expansion of its line of smart security cameras. It's releasing four new indoor and outdoor 4K cameras with (according to the company) improved viewing angles, better low-light recording, and options like true 360-degree panning and 175-degree tilt. These devices are available for purchase or preorder now, ranging in price from $70 to $220.

title: You Might Need to Replace Your iPhone 18 Pro Max
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        October 5, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Some iPhone 18 Pro Max users cannot connect to AT&T's networks. Their iPhones show an "SOS" icon in the status bar, instead.
                                            While it's not clear what's causing the issue, affected units cannot be fixed, and must be swapped out through AT&T or Apple.
                                            Unaffected units on AT&T should immediately update to iOS 27.0.1, as well as install the latest carrier update, to prevent the issue.
                                            This is just one of four major issues users are reporting with the new iPhone 18 Pro line, though this issue only affects iPhone 18 Pro Max.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Your iPhone 18 Pro Max can do a lot. It has a variable aperture that lets you control the amount of light that hits the camera sensor; it can charge up to 50% of its battery in 15 minutes (with the right adapter, of course); and it can run all of Apple's latest AI features, thanks to the new A20 processor. But the 18 Pro Max is still, above all, a phone. If it can't connect to the cellular network, you no longer have an iPhone, but a glorified iPod touch. Unfortunately, that's the situation some iPhone 18 Pro Max users find themselves in. Despite being "the best" iPhone Apple has ever made, Apple confirmed that a "small number" of 18 Pro Max units—specifically on the AT&T carrier network—can no longer connect to cellular service, with the devices only displaying an "SOS" icon at the top of their screens. That's a pretty glaring issue: Without cellular service, you'll need a wifi connection to use any apps or features that require the internet and you'll lose the ability to make calls over cellular entirely. It's so bad that some users may not even be able to call 911.  What if my iPhone 18 Pro Max can connect to cellular service right now?If your iPhone 18 Pro Max has the ability to connect to cellular service, that doesn't mean you're in the clear. Just because there's nothing wrong with your unit yet, you can still be affected by the glitch, and you'll need to install the latest update, iOS 27.0.1, as well as the latest carrier update from AT&T, to ensure your 18 Pro Max won't be affected by these mysterious cellular issues in the future. That's what Apple told 9to5Mac in the following statement: “We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls. We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today. These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.”
While you can always install iOS 27.0.1 from Settings > General> Software Update, Apple says that the carrier update will install on its own at some point over the next 14 days. However, I'd advise manually installing it by heading to Settings > General > About. There won't be any confirmation that the carrier update installs, but rest assured, this process will ensure that it has. What if my iPhone 18 Pro Max cannot connect to cellular?Unfortunately, if your iPhone is already experiencing issues connecting to cellular service, there is no fix. The updates above only help with prevention; they cannot patch an iPhone 18 Pro Max that already can't reach the network. Unfortunately, the only solution is to swap out the unit with either Apple or AT&T. The good news is your store will make the trade for you free of charge, as it is a hardware defect covered under warranty. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear why this issue is only affecting iPhone 18 Pro Maxes and not the standard iPhone 18 Pro, nor is it evident why only AT&T devices appear to be experiencing it. A possible point of failure: The iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a Qualcomm modem, while the iPhone 18 Pro uses Apple's proprietary C2 modem. Perhaps there's some flaw with Qualcomm's hardware specifically on the AT&T network. That's not to say the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro has been otherwise drama-free—far from it. As it happens, the 18 Pro (along with the 18 Pro Max) has also experienced three other public-facing issues since Apple launched the devices last month. First, there was an issue with phones randomly rebooting following a failed Face ID attempt; next, some users noticed their devices emitting a cracking or popping sound through the speakers. Finally, some units also appear to be losing their exterior color. If you've upgraded, I hope your fancy new iPhone is doing well.

        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple is introducing new controls to make it harder to run AI agents on your Mac.
                                            The company announced the changes in a post on its developer news forum.
                                            While details are slim, Apple criticized app developers for asking users to give Full Disk Access without understanding the implications and risks.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It appears agentic AI is all the rage: OpenAI's new agents, "Dots," rolled out this week, while Meta's Muse just passed five million downloads. Rather than just chatting with or using them to generate images, AI companies want users to start asking their bots to do things on their behalf, from managing their inboxes to ordering dinner.But agents aren't just the next logical step for AI as a technology. When implemented poorly, they can be wildly dangerous. AI agents are designed to run on their own, and, in order to do that, they often need near-total access to your devices and their data. Some people are now giving agents full use of their computers, including all of their messages, files, passwords, and accounts. That's a lot of trust, especially when it's not that difficult to "hack" one of these agents for malicious purposes with a poisoned prompt hidden on a website, which could lead your AI agent to hand hackers the keys to your bank accounts. That's no good. Apple is making it much more difficult for you to put yourself in this situation How does Apple feel about this? The company is famously behind on the software side of AI—it only rolled out its AI-powered version of Siri in September—but its AI hardware business is booming. When the AI agent craze first took off with projects like Moltbot, customers bought Mac minis in droves in order to run those programs. Now, Apple advertises its various Macs with AI at the forefront: It doesn't offer its own models like OpenAI or Anthropic, but it's making plenty of money selling you the hardware to run those models. 
Perhaps that's why Apple seems quite concerned about the AI agent trend, particularly when it comes to the data users are exposing to run these programs. Apple is all about privacy and security, and as such, I can only imagine the company watching in horror as so many users willingly hand their Macs (and all of their data) over to automated AI bots. Against that backdrop, the company posted an update on its developer forum entitled "Updates to Full Disk Access in macOS." In it, the company highlights the dangers of developers asking users to grant "Full Disk Access" permissions to an app. Apple says this function has been traditionally reserved for backup apps that need to access the entire disk to function. (After all, if your backup app can't access your entire Mac, how can it back up your entire Mac?) But now, Apple says developers are asking users to expose everything on their Macs, including messages, mail, browsing history, and more, without those users fully understanding the consequences. Apple even argues the privacy implications extend beyond the user, as communication apps that demand Full Disk Access compromise the people the user is chatting with, too. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
And Apple appears to be doing something about it: While details are slim, the company says it will introduce "additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action." I'm guessing this means that in the future, once you download an agent to your Mac, you'll have to click through a series of warnings and settings to "prove" to macOS that you really want to expose your entire Mac to the app and its AI. The company says it's doing this now, as the threat will only grow as AI agents improve and become more autonomous. The risks of AI are increasing across the boardI'm all for additional safeguards when it comes to AI. In the past, you needed some level of technical expertise to install an AI agent on your Mac. As such, you likely understood the risks involved, or willfully ignored all the warnings in order to do so. Now that running agents is as easy as installing Muse on your Mac, the barrier to entry is minimal. Anyone can do it, even if they don't fully understand what they are actually doing. As the AI industry reckons with the risks its technology poses to humanity, companies like Apple should indeed be figuring out how to protect their users from AI's current dangers—even if users can still choose to ignore those warnings.

title: Changing This Setting May Extend Your Battery Life on iOS 27
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        October 2, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Some users are reporting shorter battery life on their iPhones after updating to iOS 27. Connectivity Assist could be the culprit.
                                            Connectivity Assist, formerly Wi-Fi Assist, taps into your cellular network when your wifi connection is weak or unusable.
                                            The process may be putting a strain on battery life, though it's not entirely clear why.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you might have already put Siri AI to the test or tried out some of Apple's AI-powered photo editing features. But you may have also noticed something else: Your iPhone's battery isn't lasting as long between charges. While I can't say this is a universal experience (I'm don't believe my iPhone is dying faster on iOS 27 than it did on iOS 26), some users are adamant the update has had a detrimental effect on their battery life. And while there are many possible factors here, some think they have found the culprit: a feature called Connectivity Assist.   What is Connectivity Assist?Connectivity Assist's mission is noble. The feature is designed to tap into cellular data any time your wifi connection grows too weak. In theory, it should be particularly useful when you're leaving an area with wifi; rather than deal with the slow loading times a weak wifi connection forces you to endure before it disconnects outright, your cellular network would kick in to maintain your speed. (Once you've left wifi range, you'd be back on cellular completely either way, of course.)Technically, this feature isn't new. Before iOS 27, Apple called it "Wi-Fi Assist," but it worked a bit differently. In iOS 26, Wi-Fi Assist simply switches over to cellular when your wifi signal is too weak. With iOS 27's Connectivity Assist, it seems your iPhone can tap into both networks at the same time. If so, that may play some role in why this rejiggered feature seems to be dragging down people's batteries more than it used to. 
There's another new addition with Connectivity Assist that could also be part of the problem: Unlike Wi-Fi Assist, Connectivity Assist sends DNS requests over cellular data, which can bypass the rules that ad blockers put in place to stop pop-ups from making their way into your iPhone. As such, even Apple recommends that you disable Connectivity Assist if you use an ad blocker. So, if your iPhone is constantly sending out DNS requests while on cellular data, bypassing your active ad blockers, that could be putting extra strain on your battery, too. How to disable Connectivity Assist in iOS 27Reddit user ZoteTheMitey shared their experience on the r/iPhone subreddit, claiming that their iPhone 15 Pro Max, with 89% battery health, was only lasting for three to four hours following the switch to iOS 27. Once they disabled Connectivity Assistant, they claim their battery usage time jumped to seven hours. Some users in the thread shared similar experiences, and one even claimed disabling the feature fixed an issue with their device overheating.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you want to try the potential solution yourself, here are two ways to disable Connectivity Assist: First, you can disable it on a per-network basis. To do so, head to Settings > Wi-Fi, then tap the (i) next to your network name. Here, scroll down, and make sure the toggle next to "Use Connectivity Assist" is turned off. That was, you can make sure your battery isn't experiencing faster drain when you're away from a charger—say, at a cafe you frequent.If you'd rather disable the feature globally for your iPhone, head back to the Wi-Fi settings page and ensure the toggle next to "Connectivity Assist" is set to off. Note: if this feature was previously enabled, you'll be able to see the amount of cellular data the feature has used to date, which will give you an idea of how often it has been active on your device. More data could mean more potential battery drain.

        Amazon’s October Prime Day sale has brought the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE) down to $444.99 from $529.99, its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. PCMag calls it the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.
Helping all of those AI features along is a faster Qualcomm processor that Google says improves the overall performance of this smartwatch by 20%, while RAM increases from 2GB to 3GB and storage doubles to 64GB compared with the Pixel Watch 4. As for its health hardware, Google left it largely untouched, so you still get heart rate and blood oxygen monitoring, ECG readings, skin temperature, GPS, and sleep tracking, with reportedly accurate findings. And charging shouldn’t necessarily be a nightly routine, either, with the watch lasting up to 56.5 hours in testing. Heavier use will cut into that figure, but you should still have a good chance of making it through two full days with enough power left to track your sleep overnight.

        Amazon’s October Prime Day sale is underway, and the second-generation Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones are down to $369 from $449, their lowest price to date, according to price trackers. That $80 discount makes Bose’s combination of excellent noise cancellation, long-wearing comfort, and immersive spatial audio easier to justify, particularly with stronger competition this year from models such as Sony’s WH-1000XM6. For more discounts worth considering during the sale, our ongoing October Prime Day 2026 coverage has more of the latest editor-vetted deals.Bose hasn't changed the formula much in this second generation—you still get an over-ear design with plush padding and a firm but comfortable clamp for a secure fit. The only noticeable tweak is that the frame now uses a glossy metal finish instead of a matte one, which gives it a slightly more premium feel without changing how it wears.
The feature set is broad and mostly well-executed—these headphones support Bluetooth 5.4 with multipoint pairing, so you can stay connected to a laptop and phone at the same time without juggling settings. There is also a USB-C connection for wired listening, which unlocks lossless audio, something many competitors still skip. Plus, they power on automatically when you put them on and slip into a low-power mode when left flat, which is a small quality-of-life upgrade you notice quickly in daily use. Battery life is rated at 30 hours with active noise cancellation turned on, which is in line with most premium options. Bose also lets you charge and listen through USB-C at the same time, a practical addition for long work sessions.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Performance-wise, noise cancellation holds up well across different environments, taking the edge off airplane rumble, muting bus engines, and pushing most café chatter into the background, so you don’t have to keep adjusting volume just to stay immersed, notes this PCMag review. As for the sound, these headphones deliver a rich, bass-forward profile while keeping vocals and detail intact. Tracks with heavy low-end, like electronic or hip-hop, come through with depth and punch without overwhelming the mix, and vocals sound full, though the slightly recessed midrange means guitars and some instruments don’t cut through as sharply. Also, while you do get presets and noise control modes in the companion app, the simple three-band EQ does not give you much room to fine-tune the sound.
